title: The Internet Runs on Cats and Porn. It’s About to Get Cattier and Pornier
gist: ICANN's 2026 new gTLD round — the first since 2012 — drew over 1,600 applications at $227,000 each, with Reveal Day on October 7; the piece explains the registry economics (Verisign's ~$1.5B/yr from .com, Google's $25M .app), FOMO-driven applicants like Nova/LFG (316 strings) and queer-community .meow, rule changes banning post-Reveal private auctions, and ICANN's multistakeholder model as a bulwark against a splinternet.

insights.claim: Verisign, which runs .com, earns about $1.5 billion a year essentially by keeping the registry running and reports 100% uptime over 28 years.
insights.speaker: Pete Millspaugh
insights.so_what: Registries are toll-booth businesses with recurring renewal revenue and near-zero marginal cost — a durable-moat model.
insights.quote: The registry that owns .com, Verisign, makes a billion and a half dollars every year just by keeping the lights on.
insights.locator: The registry that owns .com

insights.claim: Warren Buffett invested in Verisign in 2012, when its stock was about one-eighth of today's price.
insights.speaker: Pete Millspaugh
insights.so_what: Validates the long-run compounding of the .com registry monopoly.
insights.quote: Warren Buffett thought so too, investing in Verisign in 2012, when its stock price was about one-eighth what it is today.
insights.locator: The registry that owns .com

insights.claim: Domain value chain economics: a $27.99 .app domain at GoDaddy splits into $14 wholesale to Google's registry, a 20-cent ICANN fee, and the remainder to the registrar.
insights.speaker: Pete Millspaugh
insights.so_what: Registries capture roughly half of retail price with minimal cost; registrars compete on margin.
insights.quote: Google’s registry charges $14 wholesale, ICANN collects a 20-cent transaction fee, and GoDaddy pockets the difference
insights.locator: Insiders call the words and acronyms

insights.claim: Google paid $25 million for .app in a 2012 ICANN auction, outbidding about a dozen applicants including Amazon.
insights.speaker: Pete Millspaugh
insights.so_what: Premium generic strings command eight-figure prices and can become profitable registries.
insights.quote: Google paid $25 million for it in an ICANN auction, outbidding a dozen applicants, including Amazon
insights.locator: Insiders call the words and acronyms

insights.claim: Anguilla made nearly half its revenue last year selling .ai domains, a byproduct of the AI boom.
insights.speaker: Pete Millspaugh
insights.so_what: The AI hype cycle has created outsized sovereign revenue for a tiny ccTLD holder — a vivid second-order AI beneficiary.
insights.quote: (The small island nation made nearly half its revenue last year selling domains.)
insights.locator: At 439 pages, the English-language

insights.claim: Many of the 1,200+ new TLDs from the 2012 round flopped, raising the question of whether more extensions are needed.
insights.speaker: Pete Millspaugh
insights.so_what: Most new gTLDs are poor investments; value concentrates in a few strings.
insights.quote: The 2012 round brought us more than 1,200 new top-level domains, many of which flopped.
insights.locator: Which begs the question

insights.claim: ICANN's 2026 round is the first opportunity to apply for new top-level domains since 2012, with a $227,000 application fee per string and over 1,600 applications received by the August 12 deadline.
insights.speaker: Pete Millspaugh
insights.so_what: At ~$227K each, applications alone represent roughly $360M+ committed to new namespace, plus auction proceeds.
insights.quote: ICANN charges a $227,000 application fee for each string, to recover the cost of running the program.
insights.locator: Which begs the question

insights.claim: The application process is massively FOMO-driven because no one knows when ICANN will open another round — it took over a decade to plan this one — and once a string is taken it cannot be reclaimed.
insights.speaker: Pete Millspaugh
insights.so_what: Scarcity and uncertain future rounds push speculative over-application, inflating contention and auction prices.
insights.quote: The whole thing is massively fueled by FOMO.
insights.locator: The whole thing is massively fueled

insights.claim: Nova Registry (rebranded Link Freedom Group) planned 200 TLD applications (SuperNova200) and ultimately applied for 316 strings, funded with roughly $36 million in fees from domain investor Yoni Belousov's personal account.
insights.speaker: Pete Millspaugh
insights.so_what: Portfolio-style speculative bets on hundreds of strings mirror the 2012 Donuts playbook.
insights.quote: (In August, Nova will steal ICANN’s thunder and announce the 316 strings it applied for, including .fart.)
insights.locator: Liley calls the SuperNova200 announcement

insights.claim: In the 2012 round there were about 10 times as many private auctions as ICANN auctions, with losers typically splitting the winning bid; ICANN collected about $240 million while the largest private facilitator handled about $650 million.
insights.speaker: Pete Millspaugh
insights.so_what: Private auctions let applicants profit by losing — a 'greenmail' incentive that drove speculative applications.
insights.quote: ICANN collected about $240 million from auctions in the past round.
insights.locator: I ask Konings and Swinehart

insights.claim: The 2026 rulebook bans private resolution of contested strings after Reveal Day, closing the lucrative losers-get-paid private auction route.
insights.speaker: Pete Millspaugh
insights.so_what: Reduces the payoff from speculative applications and redirects contention proceeds to ICANN.
insights.quote: the rule book now bans private resolution after Reveal Day
insights.locator: ICANN will hold its own auctions again

insights.claim: The record ICANN auction bid was $135 million for .web by Nu Dot Com, backed by Verisign, which was then stalled by legal disputes for a decade and is only now rolling out.
insights.speaker: Pete Millspaugh
insights.so_what: Incumbent .com owner defensively bought the most plausible competitor string, then it sat unused — a moat-protection play.
insights.quote: The high-water mark at an ICANN auction was a $135 million bid for .web by Nu Dot Com, underwritten by Verisign, the .com people.
insights.locator: I ask Konings and Swinehart

insights.claim: Applicants were so secretive in the last round that some flew to meet in person and avoided Gmail out of fear of Google spying on their string plans.
insights.speaker: Pete Millspaugh
insights.so_what: Shows how competitive and information-sensitive string strategy is, including distrust of big-tech incumbents who are also applicants.
insights.quote: avoiding Gmail for fear of Google spying
insights.locator: The whole thing is massively fueled

insights.claim: Announced 2026 applicants include a .agent community seeking consortium governance of AI agent identity rather than control by a single big lab, crypto firm D3 seeking meme-coin and NFT strings like .doge and .ape, and Salesforce applying for .salesforce.
insights.speaker: Pete Millspaugh
insights.so_what: Namespace is becoming a battleground for AI-agent identity and crypto branding; who controls .agent could matter for agent authentication.
insights.quote: There’s the .agent community that wants AI agent identity to be governed by a consortium, not any one big lab.
insights.locator: There are other applicants who have announced

insights.claim: The author predicts expressive TLDs could become personal identities across the web, as already happens on Bluesky where a domain serves as the username.
insights.speaker: Pete Millspaugh
insights.so_what: Domain-as-identity would increase demand for cheap, expressive TLDs and portable handles.
insights.quote: I can imagine a future where expressive top-level domains become our personal brands, identities on the internet.
insights.locator: Which begs the question

insights.claim: dotMeow raised about $137,000 on Kickstarter (150% of goal) from nearly 2,000 backers in 40 countries and expects to pay about $55,000 to apply thanks to ICANN's Applicant Support Program.
insights.speaker: Pete Millspaugh
insights.so_what: Crowdfunding doubles as a pre-sale demand signal to registrars — a novel go-to-market for TLD launches.
insights.quote: The campaign raised about $137,000—150 percent of its goal.
insights.locator: To raise enough money to apply

insights.claim: Choosing the oblique string .meow over an overt one like .trans is strategic: it reduces commercial competition and the risk of moral objections such as Saudi Arabia's 2012 objection to .gay, since ICANN objections must concern the string itself.
insights.speaker: Pete Millspaugh
insights.so_what: String selection is a game-theoretic exercise around contention and objection risk.
insights.quote: The ICANN rules are written such that an objection must relate to the string itself, not to the organization and its values
insights.locator: Choosing a string that isn’t overtly queer

insights.claim: ICANN's Applicant Support Program financed only one applicant in 2012 but 56 have qualified in 2026, many from the Global South.
insights.speaker: Pete Millspaugh
insights.so_what: ICANN is deliberately broadening the applicant base beyond corporates, shifting namespace composition.
insights.quote: In 2012, only one applicant received financial aid through ICANN’s Applicant Support Program. This year, 56 have qualified

insights.claim: dotMeow is based in Belgium and plans a 'thin' registry with EU-held data under GDPR, deliberately staying out of US jurisdiction amid fears the US might block routing to its TLD and debates on 24-hour law-enforcement data requests.
insights.speaker: Pete Millspaugh
insights.so_what: Jurisdictional arbitrage by registries signals rising concern about US political pressure on internet infrastructure.
insights.quote: The dotMeow Foundation is based in Belgium, and it’s deliberately staying out of US jurisdiction—to the extent possible.
insights.locator: It’s not just Russia that the two

insights.claim: ICANN refused Ukraine's 2022 request to cut off Russian TLDs like .ru, applying its rule to ensure stability and security without policing content.
insights.speaker: Pete Millspaugh
insights.so_what: ICANN's neutrality is a key safeguard against weaponization of DNS in geopolitical conflicts.
insights.quote: When Ukraine asked ICANN in 2022 to shut down all traffic to Russian top-level domains, like .ru, ICANN declined.
insights.locator: The Internet Corporation for Assigned Names

insights.claim: The author argues that the US ceding control of the DNS root in 2016 may be what lets a globalized internet survive, contrary to claims it 'gave away' the internet to Russia, China and Iran.
insights.speaker: Pete Millspaugh
insights.so_what: A neutral, diffuse root reduces incentives for states to build splinternets.
insights.quote: Ironically, “giving away” US control of the root might be what allows a globalized internet to last.
insights.locator: I’m careful not to say the US gave up

insights.claim: ICANN's multistakeholder model gives governments equal footing with corporations, nonprofits and the technical community, but the author acknowledges corporations lobby more effectively than end users in authoritarian countries.
insights.speaker: Pete Millspaugh
insights.so_what: Corporate influence in internet governance persists despite the inclusive design.
insights.quote: It’s easier for corporations to lobby for their special interests than it is for smaller fish
insights.locator: Like open source and the internet itself

insights.claim: California's attorney general pushed ICANN to reject the 2019 $1.1 billion sale of .org to a private equity firm cofounded by a former ICANN CEO, which ICANN did; that firm later bought Donuts, now Identity Digital, the largest TLD owner.
insights.speaker: Pete Millspaugh
insights.so_what: Private equity is consolidating TLD portfolios, and US state jurisdiction over ICANN remains a lever.
insights.quote: the nonprofit that runs .org agreed to sell it for $1.1 billion to a private equity firm cofounded by a former ICANN CEO
insights.locator: Domain governance does retain residual ties
